notes: Every item is written for any president or candidate of either party (Rule 4). High pole is consistently 'more power to the executive / fewer checks'.

items.stem: When Congress won't pass a policy the president wants, what should the president be able to do?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party, now or in the future.
options: Wait for Congress; act alone only on how the executive branch itself runs
Act alone only in emergencies
Act alone where existing laws leave the president room to decide
Act alone through executive orders whenever the president thinks it's necessary

items.stem: If Congress passes a law funding a program the president opposes, should the president be able to refuse to spend the money?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party.
items.context: Under a 1974 law, a president can delay or ask Congress to cancel spending, but must spend it if Congress doesn't agree within 45 days.
options: No; the president must spend it as Congress directed
The president can delay it briefly while asking Congress to cancel it, as current law allows
Yes, the president can refuse to spend money on programs the president considers wasteful

facts.claim: Impoundment Control Act of 1974: rescission proposals lapse unless Congress approves within 45 days of continuous session

items.stem: Should a president be able to refuse to spend money Congress approved for each of these?
items.scope: Answer each case separately, for any president.
options: Should not be able to
Should be able to
items.notes: Mirror cases: the same rule with each side benefiting. Consistency across cases is scored separately (preregistration §6a).

items.stem: When a president declares a national emergency to use special powers, how long should it last without Congress voting to approve it?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party.
items.context: Today an emergency lasts until the president ends it, unless Congress passes a law ending it, which the president can veto.
options: No special powers until Congress votes to approve
30 days, then Congress must approve
6 months, then Congress must approve
As long as the president decides, as today

facts.claim: National Emergencies Act: emergency continues until terminated by the president or by joint resolution (subject to veto); annual renewal notice required

items.stem: Should a president be able to declare an emergency to pay for a project that Congress refused to fund?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party, and for projects you like or dislike.
options: Never; spending decisions belong to Congress
Only for a sudden threat, such as an attack, until Congress can act
Yes, whenever the president judges the need is urgent

items.stem: Should a president be able to declare an emergency to spend money that Congress refused to provide, for each of these?
items.scope: Answer each case separately, for any president.
options: Should not be able to
Should be able to

cases.text: Building a wall on the southern border

items.notes: Mirror cases: the same rule with each side benefiting. Consistency across cases is scored separately (preregistration §6a).

items.stem: Should a president be able to fire career government employees, such as scientists and analysts, for disagreeing with the president's policies?
items.scope: Career employees are hired for their skills, not appointed for their politics. Answer for any president.
options: No; they should be protected from firing over policy disagreements
Only senior employees who help make policy, not regular staff
Yes, most federal employees should be fireable at will

items.stem: Some agencies, like the Federal Reserve, are set up so the president can't fire their leaders over policy disagreements. Which comes closest to your view?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party.
options: Keep these agencies independent, and make more agencies independent
Keep the independent agencies we have
Keep only the Federal Reserve independent
The president should be able to fire any agency leader

definitions.text: The central bank of the US, which sets interest rates and oversees banks.

items.stem: Should a president be involved in deciding whether the Justice Department investigates specific people?
items.scope: Think about political opponents or critics of the president. Answer for any president of either party.
options: Never; those decisions belong to career prosecutors
The president can raise concerns, but career prosecutors decide
The president can order investigations of specific people the president believes broke the law

items.stem: Should presidents pardon their own family members, associates or political allies?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party.
options: Never; amend the Constitution to forbid it
It's legal, but presidents should almost never do it
It's acceptable when the president believes they were treated unfairly

items.stem: A candidate believes they lost an election because of fraud, but courts and election officials have confirmed the result. What should the candidate do?
items.scope: Answer for a candidate of any party, in any federal or state election.
options: Concede and accept the result
Accept the result but keep saying publicly that it was stolen
Keep fighting it, including asking legislators to overturn the result
Refuse to accept it and urge supporters to resist

items.subtopic: Checks and balances vs getting things done
items.stem: Which kind of system is closer to what you want?
items.scope: Think about the federal government in general, whichever party is in charge.

sides.label: Strong checks
sides.text: No single leader can act without others agreeing, even if needed changes take years.

sides.label: Leaders can act
sides.text: An elected leader can act quickly, even if there are fewer checks on mistakes or abuse.

options: Clearly A
Lean A
Lean B
Clearly B

items.subtopic: Checks and balances vs getting things done
items.stem: Which comes closer to your view of courts?
items.scope: Think about laws in general, including ones you like and dislike.

sides.label: Courts can overrule
sides.text: Courts should strike down laws that violate the Constitution, even when most voters support them.

sides.label: Majority rules
sides.text: When most voters clearly support a law, courts should rarely overrule it, even if the law takes away some people's rights.

options: Clearly A
Lean A
Lean B
Clearly B

items.subtopic: Checks and balances vs getting things done
items.stem: Most bills in the Senate need 60 of 100 votes to pass. What should happen to this rule?
items.scope: Answer for either party being in the majority.
options: Expand it, so nominations for judges and cabinet posts also need 60 votes
Keep it as it is
Keep it, but make senators who block a bill stay and speak on the floor
End it for some kinds of bills, such as voting rights or budget bills
End it; a simple majority should pass bills

definitions.text: Under Senate rules, ending debate on most bills needs 60 votes. A senator can otherwise delay a vote indefinitely (a filibuster).

items.notes: Positions on this rule historically flip with Senate control; watch for DIF by party.

items.subtopic: Checks and balances vs getting things done
items.stem: Suppose 51 senators but not 60 support each of these. Should the majority be able to pass it?
items.scope: Answer each case separately, whatever you think of the bill itself.
options: No; keep the 60-vote rule
Yes; let the majority pass it
items.high_pole: Yes; let the majority pass it

cases.text: A national law protecting abortion access
A law expanding mail voting nationwide
A law requiring photo ID to vote nationwide

items.notes: Mirror cases: the same rule with each side benefiting. Consistency across cases is scored separately (preregistration §6a).

items.stem: How do you feel about a president who bends or works around rules that block what voters elected them to do?
items.scope: “Rules” here means laws, court rulings and official procedures. Answer for any president of either party.
options: That is never acceptable
Acceptable only in a real emergency
Acceptable when the rules clearly stand in the way of what voters chose
The country needs a leader willing to do that

items.stem: Is violence ever justified to achieve political goals in the US today?
items.scope: This is about violence by any group, for any cause. Self-defense against an attack is not included.
options: Never
Only against a government that has seized power illegally
Sometimes, when peaceful methods have failed
items.notes: Expected to be very skewed. Kept for the issue map; may not meet discrimination criteria for scoring.

items.stem: Should Congress change the number of Supreme Court justices?
items.scope: There have been 9 since 1869. Answer whichever party would gain.
options: Yes, add justices when the party in power wants different rulings
Only as part of a bipartisan reform
No; keep it at 9
items.notes: High pole here is 'keep' (more restraint), the reverse of most NORMS items.

items.stem: Should former presidents be immune from criminal prosecution for things they did as president?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party.
items.context: In 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that former presidents have broad immunity for official acts.
options: No; they can be prosecuted like anyone else
Only for core duties set by the Constitution
Yes, for all official acts

facts.claim: Supreme Court held former presidents have absolute immunity for core constitutional acts and presumptive immunity for other official acts

items.stem: Should a president be able to punish news outlets that cover them unfairly, such as by pulling broadcast licenses or press access?
items.scope: Answer for any president of either party.
options: Never; a president should not punish outlets for their coverage
Only limit access to events like briefings, not licenses
Yes, the president can punish outlets the president believes spread falsehoods

items.stem: When a law is unclear, should courts defer to the judgment of the federal agency experts who carry it out?
items.scope: Agencies of any administration.
items.context: In 2024 the Supreme Court ended a rule that required courts to defer to agencies in many such cases.
options: Yes, courts should usually defer
Only on technical or scientific questions
No; judges should decide what the law means themselves

facts.claim: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024) overruled Chevron deference
